articles.title: UK-based InsurTech Konsileo raises €5.9 million to expand its team and integrate AI | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Konsileo, a UK-based chartered insurance broker, has closed a €5.9 million (£5 million) equity round to support its continued growth.
The equity financing was led by long-term shareholders Committed Capital, together with ACF Investors. The round follows a €3.2 million (£2.7 million) raise in April 2018 and €9.4 million (£8 million) debt and equity financing in November 2024.
Steven Harris, CEO of Committed Capital, said, “We are delighted to have completed this round and to deepen our long-standing commitment to Konsileo. John, Peter and the team have built one of the fastest-growing independent brokers in the UK, and they have done it organically, broker by broker, rather than through acquisition.
“That growth rests on two things that are very hard to replicate: a proprietary broking platform that strips out administration, embeds compliance and is now putting AI to work for brokers, and a culture that consistently attracts the most talented people in the industry. Konsileo is showing what a modern commercial broker looks like, and we look forward to supporting the team through its next phase of growth.”
Founded in 2017 by John Warburton and Peter Henderson, Konsileo was born out of the shared experiences of its founders, who saw the sector as slow to modernise and overly bureaucratic. Warburton, with a career spanning senior roles at Aviva, Accenture and Allianz, has built Konsileo around what the company calls a “Teal” organisational model, replacing conventional management hierarchies with self-managed teams, coaching, and decentralised decision-making. Henderson, on the other hand, is a technologist who was at the helm of web digitisation in the 1990s, bringing platform-building expertise.
Konsileo now employs more than 220 people and arranges more than €100.5 million (£85 million) in annual insurance premiums for businesses across the UK, covering sectors from construction and healthcare to technology and professional services.
At the core of Konsileo’s offering is a proprietary, in-house broking platform that automates administrative tasks, embeds compliance checks, and helps brokers capture higher-quality risk information for clients. The firm also runs Riskube, a custom online insurance and risk management platform that enables clients to access and manage their policies directly.
Konsileo says the platform has one main goal: to free brokers from administrative tasks so they can focus on client relationships and professional advice. The model also avoids the growth-by-acquisition playbook, instead recruiting brokers one at a time and investing in their development through the Konsileo Academy.
Warburton, co-founder and CEO, Konsileo, said, “We’ve always believed that great brokers do their best work when you give them autonomy, equip them properly and support them rather than manage them. Our growth is a testament to what happens when you offer something genuinely different to ambitious brokers who want to build brilliant client relationships.”
Konsileo will use the funding to continue to attract experienced broking professionals, develop its technology platform further by integrating AI capabilities, and sustain the organic growth momentum the company has built since its inception.

articles.title: Rabatte von bis zu 42 Prozent: Lohnen sich die Xiaomi-Angebote zu den Prime Deal Days?
articles.text:
Prime Deal Days: Amazon wirbt mit günstigen Xiaomi-Smartphones – doch wie gut sind die Angebote?
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Am 6. und 7. Oktober finden die Prime Deal Days statt. Für alle, die ein neues Smartphone suchen, könnte das eine gute Gelegenheit zum Sparen sein, denn die anhaltende Speicherkrise hat die Preise bei vielen Herstellern spürbar steigen lassen. Auch zahlreiche Xiaomi-Geräte sind reduziert – laut Amazon um bis zu 42 Prozent. Wir haben die Angebote überprüft und verraten dir, bei welchen Geräten du wirklich sparst.
Poco C95 Pro: Wie gut ist der Amazon-Deal?
Das Xiaomi Poco C95 Pro soll sich für alle eignen, die eine sehr lange Akkulaufzeit und robuste Alltagshardware zu einem günstigen Preis suchen. Poco gehört wie Redmi zum Xiaomi-Konzern und nutzt das Betriebssystem HyperOS, tritt inzwischen aber auch als eigenständige Marke auf. Der Akku mit 7.500 Milliamperestunden hält laut Hersteller bei Musikwiedergabe bis zu 91 Stunden durch. Dank Schnellladefunktion sollen schon 35 Minuten Ladezeit für den ganzen Tag reichen.
Das Display misst 6,9 Zoll, die Hauptkamera löst mit 50 Megapixeln auf. Das günstige Modell setzt auf das 4G-Netz. 5G unterstützt es nicht. Im Xiaomi-Shop kostet das Poco C95 Pro mit acht Gigabyte RAM und 256 Gigabyte Speicher aktuell 329,90 Euro. Bei Amazon zahlst du während der Prime Deal Days nur 229,90 Euro. Die Ersparnis beträgt demnach 30 Prozent – wie von Amazon angegeben.
So viel sparst du jetzt beim Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G
Das Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G ist ein Mittelklasse-Smartphone für alle, die sich ein großes Display und eine lange Akkulaufzeit wünschen. Der moderne Silizium-Karbon-Anoden-Akku bietet eine besonders hohe Energiedichte und soll bei moderater Nutzung rund zweieinhalb Tage durchhalten. Das Smartphone unterstützt Schnellladen und lässt sich in Notfällen als Powerbank nutzen. Das 6,8 Zoll große Display gilt als besonders robust und augenschonend. Die Zweifach-Hauptkamera mit 50 Megapixeln soll dank optischer Bildstabilisierung verwackelungsfreie Aufnahmen liefern.
Das Modell mit acht Gigabyte RAM und 512 Gigabyte internem Speicher ist im Rahmen der Prime Deal Days aktuell für 349,90 Euro erhältlich. Laut Amazon entspricht das einem Rabatt von 42 Prozent gegenüber der unverbindlichen Preisempfehlung. Auch beim Hersteller ist das Smartphone deutlich reduziert, startet bei gleicher Ausstattung aber erst bei 449,90 Euro und liegt damit 100 Euro über dem Amazon-Angebot. Der tatsächliche Rabatt fällt also kleiner aus als beworben. Trotzdem handelt es sich nicht um einen schlechten Deal: Laut Preisvergleichsportalen ist der Amazon-Deal der günstigste Preis seit Einführung des Modells.
Poco F9 Ultra: Neu – und schon reduziert
Wer nach Flaggschiff-Leistung sucht, aber nicht in ein teures Gerät von Apple oder Samsung investieren will, findet im Xiaomi Poco F9 Ultra eine gute Alternative. Es bietet ein 6,9-Zoll-Display und einen Akku mit 8.050 Milliamperestunden, der laut Herstellerangaben mit nur einer Ladung mehr als eineinhalb Tage durchhalten soll. Mit einer Bildwiederholfrequenz von 185 Hertz und dem Prozessor Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 eignet es sich auch für Gaming und Streaming. Als erstes Modell des Herstellers verfügt es zudem über eine 200-Megapixel-Kamera.
Zusätzlich ist das Smartphone mit symmetrischen Stereolautsprechern von Bose ausgestattet. In Deutschland ist das Poco F9 Ultra erst seit September auf dem Markt. Im Xiaomi-Store ist die Variante mit 16 Gigabyte RAM und 512 Gigabyte Speicher derzeit ausverkauft, würde hier aber 1.199 Euro kosten. Bei Amazon ist das Modell aktuell um 29 Prozent auf 849,90 Euro reduziert. Bei dem brandneuen Smartphone kannst du also schon jetzt knapp 350 Euro sparen.

articles.title: Mega Oferta Prime: 5 ofertas tech imperdíveis hoje
articles.text:
A Mega Oferta Prime 2026 segue firme na Amazon até 11 de outubro, com novas ondas de produtos entrando em desconto a cada dia. Reunimos mais 5 ofertas tech imperdíveis para você aproveitar — todas exclusivas para membros Amazon Prime —, cobrindo smartphone flagship, Smart TV 4K 50″ com IA, monitor gamer IPS 144Hz, power bank robusto e headset gamer. Descontos chegam a 48% OFF.
Todas as ofertas da seleção são exclusivas Prime — para aproveitar, é necessário ser membro Amazon Prime (saiba como virar assinante no final deste artigo). A seguir, cada oferta com especificações, preço, desconto e para quem é indicada.
As 5 melhores ofertas Prime de hoje
LG UltraGear Monitor Gamer 27″ 27G411B — IPS 144Hz Nativo, 1ms, Full HD, HDR10, NVIDIA G-SYNC e AMD FreeSync — Preto
O LG UltraGear 27G411B é um monitor gamer de 27 polegadas com painel IPS — combina a precisão de cores do IPS (importante para jogos narrativos, criação de conteúdo e trabalho com imagens) com a fluidez de 144Hz nativos e tempo de resposta de 1ms, essenciais para jogos competitivos. Compatibilidade dupla com NVIDIA G-SYNC e AMD FreeSync elimina tearing em qualquer GPU.
Principais características:
- Painel IPS de 27 polegadas (cores precisas e amplos ângulos de visão)
- Taxa de atualização nativa de 144Hz (fluidez máxima em jogos rápidos)
- Tempo de resposta de 1ms (MBR) para FPS e battle royales
- Resolução Full HD 1920×1080 (ideal para GPUs intermediárias)
- Suporte a HDR10 para contraste e cores aprimorados
- Compatibilidade com NVIDIA G-SYNC e AMD FreeSync
- Design minimalista UltraGear com bordas finas
Indicado para: gamers que querem monitor IPS com alta taxa de atualização por preço competitivo, criadores de conteúdo que precisam de cores precisas, setup profissional com uso misto (jogos + trabalho), upgrade de monitor antigo 60Hz.
Motorola Edge 70 5G Crystals by Swarovski — 512GB, 12GB RAM + 12GB RAM Boost, Tela AMOLED 120Hz — Cloud Dancer
O Motorola Edge 70 5G Crystals by Swarovski é a versão especial do novo flagship da Motorola com acabamento premium decorado com cristais Swarovski. É um dos smartphones mais finos do mercado em 2025, com configuração de topo e preço significativamente reduzido no evento.
Principais características:
- Design ultrafino com cristais Swarovski aplicados
- Armazenamento generoso de 512GB
- 12GB de RAM física + 12GB de RAM Boost (virtual)
- Sistema de 3 câmeras principais de 50MP (sensor Sony)
- Tela Extreme AMOLED de 120Hz com cores vibrantes
- Conectividade 5G
- Cor Cloud Dancer (branco perolado com reflexos cristalinos)
Indicado para: quem busca smartphone premium com design diferenciado, usuários que valorizam estética Swarovski (presente ou uso próprio), armazenamento robusto para fotografia e vídeo em alta qualidade, uso prolongado por 3-4 anos.
Smart TV 4K 50″ LG UHD 50UA85 — Processador α7 AI Gen8, 4K Super Upscaling, Alexa Integrado e WebOS 25
A LG 50UA85 50″ é a Smart TV 4K da linha premium LG 2025 com processador de inteligência artificial α7 AI de 8ª geração — mesmo chip da linha PRO LG, que entrega upscaling automático de conteúdos para quase 4K, otimização de imagem por reconhecimento de cena e integração completa com assistentes de voz. Tela de 50 polegadas ideal para sala pequena a média.
Principais características:
- Painel 4K UHD de 50 polegadas
- Processador α7 AI 8ª geração com 4K Super Upscaling (melhora conteúdo em HD/Full HD para quase 4K)
- Sistema webOS 25 (interface mais recente da LG, mais fluida)
- Alexa integrada nativamente (comandos de voz sem precisar de Echo externo)
- Google Cast integrado para espelhamento sem apps externos
- Controle AI Smart Magic (apontar e clicar como mouse na tela)
- Inclui 90 dias de Amazon Music grátis
Indicado para: sala pequena a média como TV principal, usuários que querem o processador AI mais recente da LG em tela compacta, integração com casa inteligente via Alexa, cinéfilos que apreciam upscaling de qualidade em conteúdo HD antigo.
Havit Headphone H2002d — Headset Gamer com Microfone, Falante 53mm e Compatibilidade Multi-Plataforma
O Havit H2002d é um dos headsets gamer mais vendidos da Amazon no Brasil com mais de 27 mil avaliações — combina preço acessível com qualidade sonora adequada para jogos competitivos e casuais. Compatível com múltiplas plataformas via plug 3.5mm.
Principais características:
- Falantes de 53mm (acima da média da categoria, graves marcantes)
- Microfone direcional integrado para chat de voz
- Conexão por plug 3,5mm universal
- Compatível com Xbox One, PlayStation 4/5, PC, notebook, celular
- Acabamento acolchoado em espuma com memória
- Design acolchoado para longas sessões de jogo
- Cabo robusto trançado
Indicado para: gamers de entrada a intermediários, uso em consoles e PC, chat de voz em jogos competitivos (CS2, Fortnite, Valorant, FC27), presente para adolescentes gamers, segunda opção para quem já tem fone premium.
Baseus Power Bank EnerFill FC51 Bipow2 Pro — 20.000mAh, 22,5W com Display Digital e Cabo Embutido — Preto Cósmico
O Baseus Power Bank EnerFill FC51 Bipow2 Pro é um carregador portátil completo da Baseus — marca consolidada em acessórios de carregamento. Combina alta capacidade com cabo embutido (não precisa carregar cabo separado), carga rápida e display digital preciso.
Principais características:
- Capacidade de 20.000mAh (carrega smartphone até 5 vezes)
- Potência de 22,5W com carga rápida PD/QC
- Cabo USB-C embutido na própria power bank (não requer cabo externo)
- Display digital preciso mostrando porcentagem exata de bateria
- Múltiplas saídas (USB-A, USB-C) para carregar 2 dispositivos simultaneamente
- Compatível com iPhone, Android, iPad, notebooks USB-C
- Cor Preto Cósmico com acabamento refinado
Indicado para: viagens frequentes (uma carga atende dia inteiro de uso intenso), uso profissional em campo (jornalistas, representantes comerciais), estudantes universitários, nômades digitais que trabalham remoto, acompanhamento em festivais e eventos externos.
Como ser membro Amazon Prime e aproveitar as ofertas exclusivas
Para aproveitar as ofertas exclusivas da Mega Oferta Prime, é necessário ser assinante do Amazon Prime — o programa de benefícios da Amazon que inclui muito mais do que descontos. A assinatura dá acesso a frete GRÁTIS em milhões de produtos vendidos pela Amazon, biblioteca completa do Prime Video (filmes, séries e documentários originais), Prime Music (2 milhões de músicas sem anúncios), Prime Reading (centenas de eBooks), Prime Gaming (jogos e conteúdo exclusivo mensal), Amazon Photos (armazenamento ilimitado de fotos) e cupons exclusivos durante o ano todo.
A assinatura mensal custa R$ 19,90/mês ou R$ 169/ano (equivalente a R$ 14/mês no plano anual), e novos assinantes ganham 30 dias de teste grátis — tempo suficiente para aproveitar toda a Mega Oferta Prime 2026 sem compromisso. Ao final do período de teste, você pode cancelar sem custos ou manter a assinatura.
Começar teste grátis de 30 dias do Amazon Prime
Como escolher entre essas ofertas
As 5 ofertas cobrem perfis tech bem distintos. Para quem busca smartphone premium com design exclusivo Swarovski e armazenamento robusto (512GB), o Motorola Edge 70 Crystals é a maior queda percentual da lista (48% OFF, metade do preço original). Para setup gamer intermediário com monitor IPS 144Hz nativo e tempo de resposta de 1ms, o LG UltraGear 27″ é oportunidade excepcional. Para renovar TV de sala pequena/média com modelo 4K premium LG 2025 com processador AI de 8ª geração, a 50UA85 traz tecnologia topo de linha. Para gamers de entrada que querem headset confiável para consoles e PC, o Havit H2002d é escolha certeira. E para uso diário em viagens e trabalho remoto com power bank de alta capacidade e cabo embutido, a Baseus 20.000mAh resolve com cupom adicional.
Perguntas frequentes sobre a Mega Oferta Prime
Até quando dura a Mega Oferta Prime 2026?
A Mega Oferta Prime 2026 acontece de 5 a 11 de outubro — 7 dias de descontos exclusivos para membros Amazon Prime. Novas ofertas entram ao longo do período, com algumas em tempo limitado durante o dia. Vale conferir a página de ofertas em diferentes momentos para pegar as melhores oportunidades antes do fim do evento.
O que é o cupom MEGAOFERTA10 e como funciona?
O cupom MEGAOFERTA10 dá 10% OFF adicional em diversos produtos participantes do evento Mega Oferta Prime. Para usar, basta copiar o código, inserir no campo “cupom” no checkout antes de finalizar a compra. O desconto aparece diretamente no total. É cumulativo com os descontos Prime já aplicados — algumas ofertas desta seleção (Philco Aspirador, Ninja Creami e Baseus) podem ter o preço ainda menor com o cupom. Vale sempre tentar aplicar no checkout.
Monitor IPS 144Hz vs VA ou TN para jogos: qual escolher?
Depende do tipo de jogo. O painel IPS (do LG UltraGear desta oferta) entrega as melhores cores e ângulos de visão amplos — ideal para jogos narrativos (RPG, aventura), criação de conteúdo e trabalho com imagens. O painel VA tem contraste superior e pretos mais profundos — bom para jogos cinematográficos e assistir filmes. O painel TN tem tempo de resposta mais rápido e menor latência — tradicionalmente escolhido por e-sports competitivos. Hoje, com IPS atingindo 1ms (como o 27G411B), a vantagem do TN diminuiu bastante. Para uso misto (gaming + conteúdo + trabalho), IPS vale cada real; para exclusivamente FPS competitivo profissional, TN ainda tem vantagens pontuais.
Motorola Edge 70 Crystals vs Motorola Edge 70 padrão: vale a diferença?
Depende do seu gosto por design diferenciado. O Edge 70 Crystals by Swarovski (desta oferta) traz cristais Swarovski aplicados no acabamento Cloud Dancer (branco perolado) — item colecionável com apelo estético. O Edge 70 padrão tem configuração igual (512GB/12GB RAM, câmera 50MP Sony, AMOLED 120Hz) por preço similar nas versões em cores padrão. Para quem valoriza design exclusivo e apelo colecionável, Crystals vale cada real; para uso essencial sem priorizar estética premium, versão padrão atende identicamente.
Power bank 20.000mAh com cabo embutido vale a pena vs modelos sem cabo?
Sim, para a maioria dos usuários. A grande vantagem de power bank com cabo embutido (como a Baseus desta oferta) é a praticidade — você não precisa carregar cabo separado, basta puxar o cabo integrado e conectar ao celular. Elimina o problema comum de esquecer o cabo em casa. Modelos sem cabo embutido custam R$ 20-40 a menos mas exigem que você sempre leve um cabo USB-C. Para uso em mochila, bolsa e viagens, cabo embutido se paga em conveniência.
Headset Havit vs HyperX, Logitech ou Razer: qual escolher?
Depende do orçamento. O Havit H2002d (desta oferta, R$ 169,99) é a opção de entrada com qualidade decente para preço — atende bem gamers casuais e intermediários. HyperX, Logitech e Razer trazem opções premium (R$ 300-700) com drivers de maior qualidade, cancelamento de ruído do microfone e integração com softwares de áudio. Para gamers casuais com orçamento apertado, Havit atende excelente; para streamers profissionais ou gamers competitivos, vale investir em marca premium.
Vale assinar o Prime só pela Mega Oferta?
Sim, especialmente aproveitando o teste grátis de 30 dias para novos assinantes. Você pode assinar antes de uma compra grande (como smartphone ou eletrodoméstico), aproveitar o preço exclusivo Prime, usufruir dos benefícios (Prime Video, frete grátis, etc) durante o teste e cancelar antes do fim do período — sem pagar nada. Para quem compra 2-3 vezes por ano na Amazon, o plano anual (R$ 14/mês) se paga rapidamente só em frete grátis.
Os preços e a disponibilidade dos produtos mudam com frequência durante a Mega Oferta Prime, então não deixe para depois. Acesse os links, compare os modelos e aproveite os descontos enquanto eles ainda estão disponíveis — a promoção vai até 11 de outubro.

articles.title: Everything announced at Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra event
articles.text:
Microsoft just wrapped up a big Windows and Surface-focused keynote in San Francisco.
The biggest announcement was arguably the release details about the Surface Laptop Ultra, its new laptop that’s powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark Arm-based chip. The machine will start at $2,599 for a configuration with an 8-core CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage, and it will be released on October 16th. The laptop also has built-in magnetic USB-C charging instead of the proprietary Surface Connect magnetic charging port. The Verge’s Tom Warren published a deep dive all about the new laptop. Microsoft also announced that the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a mini PC for developers, is available for preorder for $5,999 ahead of shipping in November.
In addition, Microsoft shared details about some updates coming to Windows, including “Hybrid Intelligence” features that lets Copilot use files on your Windows PC to take actions and a new search experience that lets you do quick actions from the search bar.
You can catch up with all of our coverage from the event right here.
- Pinned How Microsoft built its MacBook Pro competitor Before Microsoft releases a laptop to the public, it needs to put the device through its paces. That all happens inside a windowless, warehouse-like lab on the company’s Redmond, Washington, campus, where the team developing Surface devices programs robots to press their buttons thousands of times, pelts devices with radio waves from giant antennas, and builds contraptions that drop objects from increasingly daring heights to see whether the products can hold up. Its latest laptop, the product I’m here to see, really needs to hold up. The Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t just another high-end config of the Surface Laptop, it’s the debut platform for Nvidia’s RTX Spark — Nvidia’s entrance into the world of Arm-based PC chips, and a chance to blow expectations out of the water when it comes to what a Windows laptop is capable of. Read Article >
- The first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops cost up to $7,000 The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match. Read Article >
- Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS. It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently. To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached. Read Article >
- Tom Warren and Emma Roth The Surface Laptop Ultra finally has a release date — and a starting price of $2,599 Months after revealing its Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft has announced that the Nvidia RTX Spark-equipped device will launch on October 16th. Pricing starts at $2,599 for the base configuration, featuring an 18-core CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. The Surface Laptop Ultra ships with a 15-inch HDR touchscreen display with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, along with a larger trackpad that supports haptic feedback. The device uses Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, an Arm-based processor with up to 128GB of unified memory. Both Microsoft and Nvidia are positioning RTX Spark laptops at the very premium end of the laptop market, designed for high performance across creative software, gaming, and local AI tasks. Read Article >
- Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder for $5,999 Microsoft’s Nvidia-powered Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder now and is slated to ship in November for just about $6,000. It’s pricier than the DGX Spark mini PC Nvidia launched last year, but PC prices have been climbing due to shortages of RAM and other components. The Dev Box’s flat, 3D-printed anodized aluminum chassis doubles as a heatsink and resembles the top vents on an Xbox Series X. It was introduced alongside the new Surface Laptop Ultra and runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform and 128GB of unified memory. With that much memory, along with a 100-watt thermal envelope and Nvidia’s Tensor cores, you could probably get an impressive gaming experience on the Dev Box. But as its name suggests, it’s mainly aimed at developers. It’s optimized for running local AI, including “models exceeding 120B parameters,” for tasks like testing AI models, prototyping AI agents, or running AI coding tools on-device. Read Article >
- Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra has built-in magnetic USB-C charging Microsoft has created a magnetic charging solution for its Surface Laptop Ultra that uses USB-C. After scrapping its proprietary Surface Connect magnetic charging on its smaller Surface devices last year, the Surface Laptop Ultra has a charging cable that attaches magnetically to the right side USB-C port. During Microsoft’s Windows event on Wednesday, Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri said that you can just “bring the connector close, and it snaps right into place.“ It’s still a proprietary solution, but the USB-C port it slots into still works for video, data, and other USB-C connectivity like you’d expect. Microsoft is calling it Magnetic Connect, and I’m surprised the company hasn’t shortened that to Mag-C. Read Article >
- Muse is coming to Windows. Meta’s new AI agent will be getting a native app on Windows, Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri announced at today’s event. No timeline on when, though. Meta launched a Mac Muse app in September.
- Windows and Surface live blog: On the ground at Microsoft’s event We’re in San Francisco today to hear what’s next for Windows and Surface. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri will all be holding a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.” Microsoft and Nvidia have been working together on the new RTX Spark platform, which is focused on boosting local AI models, creative apps, and even gaming on a series of new laptops. Nvidia’s GPU expertise is getting squeezed into laptops like the Surface Laptop Ultra, and we’re about to find out exactly what it’s capable of. Read Article >

articles.title: The full lineup of interactive roundtables at Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is seven days away, bringing 10,000+ founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders to Moscone West in San Francisco from October 13-15 for three days of conversations, connections, and ideas shaping what comes next.
Included in your Disrupt pass, which you can currently save $100 on, plus 50% off a second, you’ll have the opportunity to take part in a series of interactive, deep-dive roundtables, where you’ll join founders, investors, operators, and industry experts tackling the same challenges you are. Bring your questions, share your experience, and get practical perspectives on everything from fundraising and AI to hiring, enterprise software, physical AI, and scaling a company.
Don’t miss the chance to spark meaningful connections in roundtables and throughout the event. Register now to save up to $100 on your pass and get a second pass at 50% off.
Explore the full roundtable agenda lineup
This year’s sessions run across two dedicated roundtable spaces throughout Disrupt. Here’s the full lineup currently on the agenda. Explore the Disrupt agenda to learn more about all the sessions.
Arm Wrestling Your Data: The Physical AI Challenge
Radha Basu, Founder and CEO, iMerit
Physical AI needs more than bigger models. Basu explores the data challenges behind robotics and autonomous systems, including edge cases, multimodal data, and building pipelines that can operate reliably in the real world.
Is SaaS Dead? AI Is Exposing What Enterprise Software Got Wrong
Rajeev Singh, CEO, Smartsheet

articles.title: Senso to be acquired by New York-based marketing platform Zeta Global | BetaKit
articles.text:
New York-based marketing platform Zeta is looking to boost its in-house generative engine optimization (GEO) capabilities by acquiring Toronto-based Senso.
The news: Zeta Global announced on Monday that it has agreed to acquire Senso. The deal will bring Senso’s technology, which had been powering Zeta’s GEO offering, in-house. The company will also bring in the Senso team, including co-founder and CEO Saroop Bharwani, giving Zeta additional AI engineering talent, the company said in a statement. The purchase price was not disclosed.
The marketing platform said Senso will help advance its AI trust and discoverability offerings as AI assistants become an increasingly important form of customer discovery, including how brands appear in AI platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI overviews.
From the source: “Together with Zeta, we can combine Senso’s AI capabilities with Zeta’s proprietary data and customer intelligence to help businesses understand who AI is reaching, improve how they appear in AI-generated answers, and connect those insights to measurable outcomes,” Bharwani said in a statement.
The context: Founded in 2017 by Bharwani and CTO Thomas Nelson, Senso got its start providing financial institutions, particularly credit unions, with predictive intelligence tools meant to help with customer retention.
By 2022, Bharwani wasn’t sure the company would last, he said in a LinkedIn post following the Zeta deal. In 2024, Senso joined the famed Silicon Valley accelerator Y Combinator, and less than a year later unveiled a GEO tool to help credit unions become more visible and evaluate how information about them appears on AI-powered search platforms.
Final thought: As more consumers turn to AI chatbots over conventional search engines, GEO and AI-powered search optimization have replaced the once-dominant search engine optimization (SEO) for marketers. A study by SEO marketing agency Eight Oh Two earlier this year found that 37 percent of consumers used AI tools to begin a web search rather than a traditional search engine, while 47 percent of consumers used AI to help make a purchase decision.
Feature image courtesy Senso on LinkedIn.

articles.title: De Sheinbaum a Meloni: las líderes mundiales impulsan medidas para protegerse de los ‘deepfakes’ con IA
articles.text:
De Sheinbaum a Meloni: las líderes mundiales impulsan medidas para protegerse de los ‘deepfakes’ con IA
La presidenta mexicana acelera una reforma para penalizar el uso de vídeos falsos en los que aparecen funcionarios gubernamentales, mientras que la mandataria italiana patenta su voz como marca sonora ante la UE
Jefes de Estado y políticos de todo el mundo están impulsando medidas para protegerse de los deepfakes creados con inteligencia artificial. Algunos promueven normativas que abarcan a todos los funcionarios de sus respectivos países. Otros se limitan a aplicar medidas para evitar que se clonen sus voces. Estas disposiciones echan a andar al tiempo que ha trascendido que al menos 46 diputadas del Parlamento Europeo, una de cada seis, han aparecido en imágenes pornográficas hiperrealistas pero falsas de pornografía creada con inteligencia artificial, según una investigación de la organización Agora Digitale Transformation, presentada el lunes en el Parlamento Europeo. Una situación “intolerable y deplorable”, ha denunciado presidenta de la Eurocámara, Roberta Metsola, que ha urgido a los Estados miembros que garanticen la aplicación efectiva de las nuevas normas europeas, que actúen contra las aplicaciones que permiten crear este tipo de contenido y que se persiga la difusión de deepfakes sexuales no consentidos.
En Italia, la primera ministra Giorgia Meloni ha solicitado registrar su voz como marca ante la Unión Europea con el objetivo de defenderse de montajes realizados con inteligencia artificial. Según ha adelantado este lunes el periódico La Repubblica, la ultraderechista ha archivado su voz y las inflexiones de su timbre ante la Oficina de Propiedad Intelectual de la Unión Europea (EUIPO) con una grabación de cuatro segundos en la que pronuncia dos veces la frase Io sono Giorgia Meloni (Yo soy Giorgia Meloni). La solicitud sigue en fase de revisión, pero, si es aceptada, Meloni dispondrá de nuevas herramientas legales para impedir la circulación de contenidos falsos, como exigir la retirada de cualquier material ilícito y reclamar posteriormente una indemnización por daños.
Elena Gil, abogada experta en IA y fundadora de Data Guardians, advierte de que registrar la voz no ofrece una cobertura absoluta frente a la generación de vídeos falsos: “Es verdad que la marca puede ayudar a determinados usos comerciales, pero como la protección se da para los productos o servicios para los que tú la hayas registrado, no es para cualquier deepfake”, explica.
Si bien Meloni ha optado por una herramienta de protección individual, en México, en cambio, el Gobierno trabaja en una medida mucho más amplia que no solo protege a la presidenta, Claudia Sheinbaum. El pleno del Senado aprobó el miércoles último, por 72 votos a favor y 34 en contra, una reforma para penalizar el uso de vídeos falsos en los que aparecen funcionarios gubernamentales. La modificación, que aún debe aprobarse por la Cámara de Diputados, ha sido bautizada como “ley anti-memes” y ha despertado duras críticas por parte de la oposición. Los parlamentarios acusaron a la administración de Sheinbaum de crear un instrumento para censurar la sátira y la parodia, al reformar la Ley Federal de Protección a la Propiedad Industrial y el Código Penal federal.
Ante el revuelo generado, la propia jefa de Estado ha intentado contener la polémica. “¿Qué se sanciona? Que salga la presidenta en un video utilizando inteligencia artificial para cometer un fraude. Eso es lo que aparece en la ley, que no se pueden cometer delitos. No la sátira política, ni siquiera la ofensa personal”, explicó en la conferencia matutina del jueves pasado. La consejera jurídica del Ejecutivo Federal, Luisa María Alcalde Luján, detalló que el texto aprobado contempla una pena de cinco años de cárcel y una multa de hasta 1.173.000 pesos mexicanos (unos 58.000 euros).
Para el abogado experto en derecho digital Borja Adsuara, medidas como las impulsadas por Claudia Sheinbaum o Giorgia Meloni no son necesarias en España, donde el adelanto electoral ha dejado de momento en suspenso la reforma que pretendía prohibir por primera vez los videos falsos generados sin el consentimiento de la persona afectada. En su opinión, no hay que regular los deepfakes como una categoría específica, como pretendía hacer el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez antes de la disolución de las Cortes con una nueva ley. “No se debe crear un nuevo derecho a la propia imagen en el entorno digital. Ya nos protege la Constitución en su artículo 18, nos ampara la ley de protección civil, el código penal y la ley de protección de datos. La imagen y la voz son datos personales”, insiste en una conversación telefónica mientras recuerda que la Agencia Española de Protección de Datos ya ha abierto expedientes sancionadores por usar la imagen y la voz de una persona sin su consentimiento.
Adsuara propone como alternativa que, en todo caso, se introduzcan agravantes a los delitos que ya están legislados y pone como ejemplo las estafas que se cometen haciendo uso de vídeos generados o manipulados. “En vez de poner deepfake, se puede poner imágenes reales o realistas. Con esa terminología, da igual si se crearon con inteligencia artificial o con Photoshop. No hay que hacer una reforma legal cada vez que nos encontramos ante una tecnología emergente”, sentencia.
Elena Gil, la divulgadora y abogada experta en IA, coincide en parte con Adsuara, aunque afirma que una normativa específica ayudará a arrojar una mayor claridad. “Una ley que mencione expresamente que las imágenes manipuladas sin consentimiento están penalizadas puede ayudar a dar más seguridad jurídica, pero eso no quiere decir que actualmente no exista una protección”, indica.
La respuesta de los gobiernos para proteger a sus autoridades o a sus ciudadanos de los peligros de la inteligencia artificial varía de país a país. Gil destaca el caso de Dinamarca. “Han aprobado una ley que otorga a los ciudadanos derechos sobre su propia identidad digital, la voz, el rostro o el cuerpo. Esto es para evitar que se usen para entrenamiento de la IA. La normativa les permite, incluso, pedir indemnizaciones. Como excepción, se permite la sátira o la parodia con fotografías o vídeos creados por IA, porque no cualquier imagen generada implica que hemos cruzado el umbral de lo que es ilegal”, apunta.
En otros países, como Brasil, las medidas se han concentrado en el ámbito electoral. En agosto, el Tribunal Superior Electoral (TSE) llegó a un acuerdo con la empresa británica ElevenLabs para crear un mecanismo de protección para bloquear la clonación no autorizada de las voces de los candidatos. Entre los aspectos clave de la asociación, figura la lucha contra la desinformación, la detección de fraude y la colaboración en investigaciones judiciales para determinar si las grabaciones de audio sospechosas de ser fraudulentas se generaron en sus propios sistemas.

articles.title: Technologie-Dilemma: Schlechte Stimmung wegen KI – dennoch eine Milliarde Nutzer von ChatGPT
articles.text:
Eine Milliarde Nutzer von ChatGPT: Dennoch hat KI ein Akzeptanz-Problem bei uns
Es ist schon komisch: Weltweit steigen die Nutzer:innen zahlen von KI-Chatbots wie ChatGPT oder Gemini, doch zugleich liegt eine negative Stimmung gegenüber KI in der Luft. Mir wurde das an folgender Situation in diesem Sommer bewusst: Ich konnte mit dem CEO des Startups Springboards sprechen, einer Firma, die ein LLM entwickelt, das eine größere Vielfalt an Antworten liefern soll als die etablierten Konkurrenten mit ihren Modellen von Claude bis ChatGPT. Zu Beginn des Gesprächs sagte Pip Bingemann etwas Erstaunliches: „Wir sagen oft, dass wir ein uns selbst hassendes KI-Unternehmen sind. Wir wissen selbst nicht, ob uns das, was wir tun, wirklich gefällt.“ Meine Antwort: „Möglicherweise bin ich auch ein mich selbst hassender KI-Journalist.“

articles.title: London’s Cori Clinical raises €3.8 million to accelerate clinical trials and reduce delays | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cori Clinical, a London-based startup that acts as the intelligence layer to accelerate clinical trials, has closed a €3.8 million Seed round led by Breega, with participation from Enzo, Heartfelt, Together Ventures, and Bynd.
The company plans to use this capital to expand delivery capacity; support team growth, including appointing Chief Clinical Officer Dr. Emma Ogburn, who joins from Lindus Health; and deepen the regulatory and clinical intelligence in Cori’s platform.
Jorn Jansen Schoonhoven, co-founder and CEO of Cori Clinical, said, “Clinical trials are built through a series of interconnected decisions about how a study should be designed and run. Today, much of the knowledge and precedent behind those decisions is scattered across previous trials, siloed teams, internal systems and separate documents. Cori brings that intelligence together into a living blueprint, so teams can make better-informed decisions before avoidable problems become delays, so the science never waits on the process.”
Founded in 2025 by Schoonhoven (CEO) and Patricio Fernández (CTO), Cori Clinical creates a living blueprint of a trial from initial idea through execution.
Its unified workspace turns a clinical team’s collective insight and organisational experience, coupled with trusted external intelligence, into a single, shared source for all clinical and commercial teams. It helps teams identify risks, assess options and connect study design with the practical requirements of running
According to the company, clinical trials still rely on fragmented processes and disconnected sources of information, making it difficult for teams to apply relevant precedent and assess the wider implications of early design decisions. It notes that getting those early decisions wrong is costly. In addition to the cost incurred, amended protocols were also associated with longer recruitment and overall study durations.
“That is frustrating for everyone involved: CROs trying to run trials effectively and cost-efficiently; sponsors trying to reach ‘first participant in’ as quickly as possible; and, most importantly, patients waiting for new treatments that depend on a trial starting,” the startup mentioned in the press release.
Cori Clinical is an AI workspace which claims to bring together the knowledge an organisation has developed through years of clinical trial experience and combines it with external intelligence from clinical-trial registries, regulatory guidance and public sources, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)s, the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA).
Cori helps clinical teams turn an initial trial brief into a full protocol, submission package and operational plans, built against current regulatory guidance.
The company notes that it helps teams build and maintain a living blueprint for a feasible and executable trial, instead of addressing a single document or workflow,
As new guidance is published, the UK startup builds it into the workspace and flags the risks and decisions that matter for a trial’s success. This lets teams test proposed designs against their experience and the wider evidence base, identify risks, assess options, and link study-design decisions to budgets, timelines, and operational plans.
Based on internal modelling using average trial set-up costs, historical modification rates, and time to ‘first participant in’, Cori estimates that its approach could reduce average trial set-up costs by at least 33%.
Matthieu Vallin, Partner at Breega, which led the funding round, said, “Clinical trial start-up is a critical but often overlooked bottleneck in drug development, with months lost between designing a trial and enrolling the first patient. Cori is bringing the intelligence and connected workflows needed to make that process faster, and we’re excited to back Jorn, Patricio and Emma and the team as they bring this powerful capability to more trials”.
Cori Clinical is already working with 2 of the top 5 enterprise CROs globally. It has customers across the clinical development ecosystem, including Erasmus MC, an academic medical centre and university hospital in Rotterdam, where the Cori platform supported two clinical trials in neurosurgery and neuro-oncology.

articles.title: Athlete-led Endo launches with $815,000 to modernize sports agencies | BetaKit
articles.text:
A group of Canadian athletes has teamed up to help sports agencies streamline their operations and make more informed decisions using AI-powered software.
Toronto-based Endo officially launched on Wednesday with 11 sports agencies, including Quartexx Management, Roy Sports Group, KHG Sports Management, and Envision Sports and Entertainment, which cater to multimillion-dollar rosters of clients across the NHL, MLB, and other leagues, and $815,000 CAD in pre-seed funding led by Toronto’s Relay Ventures, Endo co-founder and CEO Michael Boushy told BetaKit in an exclusive interview.
“Agents are still running eight-figure careers out of spreadsheets. Endo gives them the number, and the system to scale.”
John Albright, Relay Ventures
After wrapping up his Western University hockey career, Boushy stayed connected to the sports world by joining a leading talent agency in Los Angeles-based The Team (formerly Wasserman). Boushy spent nearly three years with The Team as a consultant, where he negotiated athlete endorsement deals for brands and learned that the agents on the other side of the table typically relied on instinct rather than hard data, putting them at a sizeable “information gap.”
“Each marketing endorsement was very arbitrary,” he said. That realization, coupled with the insight that these talent agencies still operated in a “quite archaic” fashion, inspired Boushy to join forces with friend and fellow Western alumnus Jack Lavorato (Endo’s co-founder and COO) this summer to tackle these problems head-on. The pair has since recruited Boushy’s former junior hockey teammate, Anthony Baxter, as co-founder and founding engineer, as well as former BMO developer Matteo Tanzi as senior product engineer.
“Everyone wants to understand what their athletes are worth from a marketability standpoint, because it’s never been done before,” Boushy added. “They don’t understand the angles that a brand would typically take in justifying their price point, so we’re helping the agent find the value of their clients.”
Together, they are developing a software platform to help sports agencies modernize their operations that integrates roster management, contract tracking, and deliverable fulfillment into “a single system of record.”
Endo is also building an underlying proprietary AI valuation engine, called endodeals, that measures incoming endorsement offers from brands against media equivalency and anonymizes comparable contracts to help agents assess what their clients’ marketability and these proposals are truly worth.
RELATED: Peripheral nets $8.7 million USD to bring spatial intelligence tech to sports
“We want to become the benchmark for fair market value in the name, image, and likeness-endorsement ecosystem,” Boushy said.
Relay bought into that vision—and the Endo team’s firsthand experience in this space—via its pre-seed round, which closed in July and was raised via simple agreements for future equity.
“Talent has never been worth more, and agents have never had less time and resources at their disposal to prove it,” Relay founder and partner John Albright told BetaKit over email. “That’s the gap we believe Endo closes.”
Sponsorship spending in Canada rose 17 percent year-over-year, to $4.7 billion in 2025. A significant portion of those dollars flowed towards sports. But Boushy said many agencies still operate their businesses manually across a combination of messy, disparate spreadsheets, contracts, email chains, and memory, which can lead to missed payments, deliverables, and undervalued deals.
Boushy claims Endo’s current platform can save agents as much as 10 to 15 hours a week by centralizing all of this data and making it much easier to parse. While Endo is starting with athletes, Boushy sees potential for its tech across the talent ecosystem, from actors to celebrities, influencers, and musicians.
Feature image courtesy Endo.

articles.title: Faster Scientific Image Analysis with NVIDIA cuPhoton | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Observatories and telescopes, lasers and X-ray light sources, and other high-throughput instruments generate image data faster than CPU-bound pipelines can process it to support timely decisions. The computational bottleneck is rarely one slow kernel. It’s the whole path from data in the sensor to a decision: read the raw data, match point-spread functions or detector responses, subtract or reduce, fit, classify, and alert.
Modern facilities routinely accumulate petabytes of multidimensional data across a single survey or experiment campaign. With CPU-first implementations, it can take hours to months—sometimes a year or more—to obtain scientifically useful results from data the instrument produced in seconds. These delays make it harder for scientists and engineers to extract insights and advance their research. What is missing is a GPU-native path that covers every stage from the sensor to the decision, not a faster version of any one step.
NVIDIA cuPhoton is an open-source NVIDIA CUDA-X toolkit of GPU-accelerated building blocks for that path, spanning use cases from spectral and optical astronomy to time-domain laser/X-ray analysis. By keeping image data on the GPU from sensor read through classification, cuPhoton collapses the wait to seconds, resulting in a tight loop that researchers can run interactively, shortening time to insight and letting facilities keep pace with the data their instruments are producing.
Accelerating scientific insights from months to minutes with cuPhoton
Across astronomy, X-ray science, and other high-throughput domains, NVIDIA cuPhoton provides tools for loading, processing, and analyzing massive multidimensional datasets. The following example combines cuPhoton modules into an end-to-end workflow.
The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory is a prominent example of modern scientific facilities with high demand for fast extraction of scientific insights. Every 39 seconds after dark, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSSTCam records a new 3.2-gigapixel exposure of the southern sky. The Prompt Processing pipeline compares each frame with a reference template of the same sky region. Within about 60 to 120 seconds, it must classify roughly 10,000 detections as astrophysical transients or artifacts such as cosmic rays, satellite trails, and processing errors. Across an entire night, that amounts to up to 20 terabytes of images and 10 million candidate objects.
NVIDIA cuPhoton scales across multi-GPU, multi-node NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and NVIDIA Vera Rubin systems. On representative workloads involving hundreds of terabytes of data using multiple GPUs, cuPhoton has accelerated image loading and reading by up to 14,900x and signal processing by up to 14,550x, turning months of computational time into minutes. Data analytics that previously took nine months have been demonstrated in four hours on GPU-accelerated Python. For smaller datasets on the order of kilobytes, the entire cuPhoton pipeline executes on millisecond or even microsecond timescales. Figure 3 compares speedups for individual cuPhoton operations against an x86 CPU baseline; these results are not an end-to-end pipeline speedup.
Walkthrough of an example scientific workflow
This post walks through a realistic scientific workflow, using a physically motivated synthetic pair of astronomical images. The following examples are kept small so they can run on NVIDIA DGX Spark or a single-GPU workstation. The same workflow scales across multi-GPU workstations and clusters; that launch is shown later in this post. Figure 4 shows the workflow stages covered in the following sections.
- Load the current exposure and reference data into GPU memory.
- Align: Place both visits on a shared sky grid so the same star falls on the same pixel.
- PSF-match and subtract: Match the point-spread functions (PSFs)—the patterns that describe how light is distributed across pixels—in the current exposure and an earlier reference of the same region. Then subtract the reference. A moving object leaves a paired pattern of positive and negative pixels called a dipole.
- Fit a dual-PSF model to the dipole to estimate the moving object’s positions.
- Visualize the results: display the PSF-matching kernel, subtraction residual, and recovered dipole.
Execution of workflow
The following example uses small synthetic datasets so you can test it on your machine. Peak performance numbers quoted earlier vary by workload, dataset, implementation, and hardware. The largest speedups are individual operations and should not be read as an end-to-end pipeline factor.
This walkthrough covers five cuPhoton components: xDataReader, xRep, xPois, xFit, and xScan. The toolkit also includes xRay for time-domain X-ray detector analysis.
First, clone the repository and follow the README setup workflow. The setup command (uv sync --locked --extra dev --extra gpu --extra viz) provisions a locked Linux environment backing the NVIDIA CUDA 13 ecosystem: CuPy, PyTorch, Numba-CUDA, KvikIO, and NVIDIA nvCOMP, along with visualization libraries (Bokeh and Pillow). The same checkout includes the cuPhoton CLI, the modules used in this walkthrough, and examples/run_quickstarts.py, which generates synthetic inputs and writes run artifacts to quickstart-output/.
Set up a work directory
Follow the README to create the locked CUDA 13 GPU environment. xDataReader’s FITS path additionally needs its native extension; from the checkout run bash src/cuphoton/xdr/src/build.sh (xDataReader guide). cuPhoton 0.1.3 supports Python 3.12–3.14 and CUDA 13 on Linux.
Building xDataReader from source requires a C++17 compiler, CUDA and cuFile development headers, and a reentrant CFITSIO development installation. See the xDataReader guide for setup instructions.
git clone --branch v0.1.3 --depth 1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton.git
cd cuPhoton
export WORK_DIR="$PWD/blog-run"
mkdir -p "$WORK_DIR"/{fits,npz,figs}
Execute each Python snippet sequentially within a single interactive session (such as Jupyter, IPython, or an integrated script) starting from the root directory. Later sections reuse variables retained in memory: images, aligned, reference, target, fit, stamp, model, and result. Ensure WORK_DIR remains defined throughout execution. If the native xDataReader component is unbuilt, pause and execute bash src/cuphoton/xdr/src/build.sh.
The complete workflow script is available in the cuPhoton repository. For automated runs from a fresh terminal, invoke run_imaging_pipeline.py via uv run python. For an interactive notebook, open run_imaging_pipeline.ipynb in Jupyter.
Load FITS directly onto the GPU
The Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) is a standard data format in astronomy and astrophysics. Typically, you read the data with Astropy on the CPU and then call cupy.asarray to transfer the resulting array onto GPU memory. Parsing and decompression occur on the host, followed by a PCIe transfer before any science kernel runs. (At data rates of terabytes per hour, this sequence creates substantial data-movement overhead and is the first place the alert latency budget is consumed.)
To address this bottleneck, xDataReader accelerates decompression, reading, and loading FITS directly to the GPU. Specifically, xDataReader splits the workload as follows: CFITSIO plans byte ranges on the CPU, KvikIO reads them (NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage when available), nvCOMP decompresses GZIP tiles on the GPU, and CuPy holds the result. It supports uncompressed 2–16-axis image HDUs and two-dimensional images with GZIP_1 or GZIP_2 tile compression. Rice compression and dithered floating-point quantization are not supported.
GPUDirect Storage is available with a compatible driver and filesystem. On other CUDA 13 machines, KvikIO may take its PCIe compatibility path. The Python API does not change. batch_to_device still returns CuPy arrays; cuphoton.xdr.is_gds_active() reports the current path.
The public API is batch_to_device. It defaults to HDU index 1, the first extension, which must contain a supported image. For an image in the primary HDU, pass hdu_indices=(0,). The function returns one stacked CuPy array per requested HDU. Files grouped into one call must match in shape and dtype at each selected HDU.
Example:
The following code writes two synthetic 256×256 frames that mimic a reference template and a later science exposure: three static stars plus one fainter source that moved by a few pixels. The single moving source is the dipole you should recover after subtraction. The science frame is also a little blurrier, as if the seeing were worse. The example then shifts the science image to mimic a pointing offset and updates the header so both frames still describe the same sky. The two files do not share a detector pixel grid, but the World Coordinate System (WCS) in their headers maps both to the same sky coordinates.
The first Python block is scaffolding. Paste it once and keep the session open. It imports everything later sections need and sets WORK plus the scene constants those two FITS files were written with. The downloadable script (run_imaging_pipeline.py) writes the files with sky coordinates in the headers and defines the PNG helpers used at the end.
import os
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits
from PIL import Image
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter
from scipy.ndimage import shift as ndshift
from cuphoton.xdr import batch_to_device
from cuphoton.xfit import GaussianDipoleModel, fit_dipoles
from cuphoton.xpois import GaussianBasisComponent, solve_constant_kernel
from cuphoton.xrep import (
    BBox,
    Grid,
    build_stack_spec_from_fits,
    make_north_up_wcs,
    reproject_stack,
)
SHAPE = (256, 256)
STARS = (
    (70.0, 80.0, 45.0, 2.10),
    (175.0, 190.0, 32.0, 2.40),
    (40.0, 200.0, 22.0, 2.00),
)
MOVER_OLD = (120.0, 108.0, 14.0, 2.10)  # y, x, amp, sigma
MOVER_NEW = (126.5, 116.0, 14.0, 2.10)
CRVAL = (150.0, 2.0)
PIXEL_SCALE = 0.2  # arcsec / pixel
SCIENCE_SHIFT = (20.0, -32.0)  # dy, dx; large enough to see by eye
SEEING_SIGMA = 0.65  # extra Gaussian blur applied to the science frame
That scaffolding stays in memory. The product call is batch_to_device: it reads both image HDUs onto the GPU and returns a stacked CuPy array.
(images,) = batch_to_device(
    [WORK / "fits" / "template.fits", WORK / "fits" / "science.fits"],
    hdu_indices=(1,),
)
A successful run prints the array shape (2, 256, 256), its dtype, and the GPU device it landed on—confirming both frames made it onto the device. Those arrays are still in each file’s native pixel grid. The static stars should not line up; that is the planted mismatch, not a failure of the loader.
Interpolation and alignment: Align both visits on the same sky grid
Two visits to the same patch typically do not share a pixel grid. Dither, rotation, and plate scale put the same star on different (x, y) in the template and the science frame. The WCS in the FITS header is the map from those pixels to the sky. xPois matches point-spread functions on arrays that are already registered. Subtract first, and every static star becomes a residual; the mover is no longer a clean dipole.
xRep resamples two-dimensional images onto a shared north-up celestial grid. build_stack_spec_from_fits reads both WCS solutions and builds one destination footprint. reproject_stack warps every member onto that grid. backend="auto" prefers CuPy, then CUDA PyTorch, then CPU if no GPU is available. Interpolation is Lanczos-3 by default.
The next block keeps the FITS written above—native detector pixels plus the planted CRPIX offset—and puts both visits on one grid. After the warp, static stars should sit on the template. The mover should remain the only source that changed position in the sky.
native, spec = build_stack_spec_from_fits(
    [WORK / "fits" / "template.fits", WORK / "fits" / "science.fits"],
    hdu=1,
    grid=Grid.from_wcs(wcs_t),
    output_bbox=BBox(0, 0, SHAPE[1], SHAPE[0]),
    interpolation="lanczos3",
    mapping_grid_step=16,
)
aligned = reproject_stack(native, spec, backend="auto")
Print aligned.images.shape and aligned.backend. Expect a stack of two frames and a GPU backend on CUDA 13. If static stars still sit a few pixels apart, the WCS did not describe the shift you planted, or the destination grid did not cover both footprints.
Matching PSF and subtraction
A raw science-minus-template difference is dominated by residuals around every bright star caused by differences in atmospheric blurring (seeing). Optimal image subtraction, following Alard and Lupton, instead solves for a compact convolution kernel K and a differential background B so the reference template R acquires the science PSF and matches the science exposure, T:
T ≈ R ⊗ K + B,
where ⊗ denotes convolution. The resulting model is then subtracted from the exposure T to produce the difference D:
D = T − (R ⊗ K + B).
Using a Gaussian-polynomial kernel basis, xPois computes the convolution kernel required for optimal image subtraction. For the constant-kernel solve used here, backend="auto" selects the first available backend in this order: CuPy, Numba-CUDA, CPU. The small coefficient solve stays on the host; the pixels do not. Flux-conserving basis rewriting keeps the kernel sum near one. Check this sum when assessing flux conservation. A well-behaved kernel is compact and roughly symmetric. A bright ring or a large negative bowl means the basis cannot represent the seeing mismatch, or a saturated star entered the fit unmasked.
The next block keeps reference and target from the aligned stack and fits a 15×15 kernel. Because xRep puts the visits on one WCS, a compact kernel should absorb the seeing mismatch. The three static stars should cancel. The mover should remain as a positive lobe at t1 and a negative lobe at t0.
fit_mask = np.ones(SHAPE, dtype=bool)
fit_mask[105:142, 93:132] = False
fit = solve_constant_kernel(
    reference,
    target,
    [GaussianBasisComponent(sigma=SEEING_SIGMA, degree=0)],
    kernel_shape=(15, 15),
    background_degree=0,
    flux_conserve=True,
    fit_mask=fit_mask,
    backend="auto",
)
Print fit.backend, kernel.sum(), chi2, and fit_pixel_count. A kernel sum near 1.0 and a residual whose bright-star rings have collapsed means the match worked. If the stars still dominate D, either the images were not registered—use cuphoton.xrep to put them on a shared WCS—or the kernel basis is too narrow for the seeing difference. On a CUDA 13 GPU, fit.backend should be cupy and residual RMS should sit far below the peak star amplitude of about 45 in this scene.
Fit the dipoles
Moving objects, such as asteroids, and image-registration errors can produce dipole patterns. These are paired positive and negative flux regions in a difference image. Processing each candidate separately can become a bottleneck. A pipeline may need to solve thousands of least-squares optimization problems across small image stamps for each exposure.
In this example, xFit’s GaussianDipoleModel models each stamp as a difference between two rotated elliptical Gaussian components. Both components are evaluated at the same pixel coordinates (x,y) and share amplitude, widths, and orientation. The two centers (x⁺, y⁺) and (x-, y-) vary independently:
m(x, y) = G(x, y; x⁺, y⁺) − G(x, y; x⁻, y⁻)
xFit also supports models based on supplied sampled PSFs through StampDipoleModel.
xFit’s Levenberg–Marquardt solver factors many regularized Gauss–Newton systems at once on CuPy. Converged fits stop participating in subsequent solver iterations, reducing unnecessary work. The synchronous call returns the batch results after the remaining fits finish. Widths are optimized in log space and returned as positive pixel standard deviations; the analytic Jacobian is the default for the Gaussian model. Returned arrays are portable NumPy—parameters, covariance, and standard errors—so a classifier never imports the CuPy solver.
The following code cuts a 21×21 stamp around the planted mover in the xPois residual and starts the fit from a slightly wrong initial guess. Print the recovered centers alongside the known input positions. Compare the recovered centers with the known input positions to check fit accuracy.
STAMP = 21
half = STAMP // 2
cy, cx = 123, 112  # midpoint of the planted mover
stamp = fit.residual[cy - half : cy + half + 1, cx - half : cx + half + 1]
# Seed the fit from the observed stamp extrema, in centered x/y coordinates.
y_pos, x_pos = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(stamp), stamp.shape)
y_neg, x_neg = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(stamp), stamp.shape)
initial = np.array(
    [
        [
            stamp.max(),
            2.0,
            2.0,
            0.0,
            x_pos - half,
            y_pos - half,
            x_neg - half,
            y_neg - half,
        ]
    ]
)
model = GaussianDipoleModel((STAMP, STAMP), dtype=np.float64)
result = fit_dipoles(
    stamp[None], model=model, initial=initial, backend="auto"
)
Expect converged: True on this synthetic data. Recovered (x_pos, y_pos) and (x_neg, y_neg) should sit within a fraction of a pixel of the planted offset. A structured leftover in the fit residual usually means the stamp still contains a static star or the initial centers were on the wrong lobe.
Review the stamps
The examples above validate the workflow on a controlled synthetic scene with one planted moving object and known ground truth. Real observations provide neither that simplicity nor that certainty. A single telescope pointing (visit) can generate up to 10,000 candidates, and a full night yields millions, making individual inspection impractical. The next step is to prioritize candidates for human review.
cuphoton xscan review-queue ranks the candidates—by model uncertainty, by known errors, or as a straight dataset audit—and limits the number of candidates for human review. Use cuphoton xscan review-bokeh to inspect the search exposure (current observation), the reference template, the raw difference, and the xPois residual, with Real / Bogus / Unsure labels for each candidate.
Figure 9 shows the review interface with an example noise artifact, so you can inspect the layout before using it with an observation. Observational FITS data are not in the git repository. Copy an example under examples/xscan/, set the local paths, and follow the README plus the xScan guide to build a review queue and launch the app.
Scale the same workflow across multiple GPUs
The walkthrough above is one image pair on one GPU, small enough for an NVIDIA DGX Spark or a workstation. NVIDIA cuPhoton runs the same loading and processing path across multi-GPU, multi-node systems. After registration, cuPhoton distributes complete image pairs and their candidate coordinates across GPU workers, keeping image arrays on the device through subtraction, dipole fitting, and classification. This example uses synthetic inputs and an untrained model to verify a multi-GPU launch. Scaling that path is how the toolkit handles survey-sized streams such as Vera C. Rubin Observatory exposures. To run many pairs, use the following commands. Environment setup, Slurm and SSH launches, and the Dragon alternative are in the distributed execution guide.
python examples/distributed-pipeline/prepare_example.py \
  --output "$CUPHOTON_RUN_ROOT/input" --images 8
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES-0,1,2,3}"
mpiexec -n 8 --map-by ppr:4:node --bind-to none \
  -x CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES \
  cuphoton-openmpi-rank-exec -- \
  cuphoton xscan run-pipeline --executor mpi \
  --manifest "$CUPHOTON_RUN_ROOT/input/pipeline.json" \
  --output-dir "$CUPHOTON_RUN_ROOT/runs" --name blog-mpi \
  --warmup-rounds 1 --measure-rounds 1
--images 8 creates eight image pairs, and -n 8 starts eight MPI workers, mapped one per GPU. The pairs must already share a pixel grid, which is the xRep step above. On a machine with one GPU per node, set both numbers to the node count and use --map-by ppr:1:node. Those commands come from the distributed-pipeline example, which also includes the host-file templates. The generated model only checks that the workers start and finish.
Get started
The examples were developed on NVIDIA DGX Spark and target Linux systems with compatible NVIDIA GPUs and drivers. Follow the cuPhoton README to clone the repository, check the supported Python and CUDA versions, and set up the environment.
- Build the native xDataReader extension for FITS input: xDataReader guide.
- Run data loading and processing across multiple GPUs and nodes: distributed execution guide.
- Create a review queue and launch the candidate review interface: xScan guide.
- Explore component APIs and output artifact specifications: cuPhoton documentation.
For related examples, read Accelerated X-Ray Analysis for Nanoscale Imaging (XANI) and Using Accelerated Computing to Live-Steer Scientific Experiments at Massive Research Facilities.
Watch the NVIDIA cuPhoton product overview for an introduction to the toolkit.

articles.title: Diablo 2 en VR change complètement la façon de jouer au mythique RPG de Blizzard
articles.text:
Diablo II est sorti en 2000 et fait partie des épisodes qui ont attiré énormément de nouveaux venus dans l’univers de Diablo. Il faut dire qu’à l’époque de sa sortie, le jeu de Blizzard s’est rapidement forgé une solide réputation, au point de devenir un incontournable pour les amateurs de hack’n’slash, mais aussi pour celles et ceux qui découvraient le genre pour la première fois.
Considéré aujourd’hui comme le meilleur épisode de la licence par de nombreux fans, Diablo II revient sur le devant de la scène, entre deux actualités autour du cinquième épisode, quant à lui attendu pour 2029. Si l’on reparle de Diablo II, c’est grâce à un mod qui permet de parcourir en VR Diablo II: Resurrected, le remaster sorti en 2021.
Des images de ce mod ont été partagées sur Reddit le 5 octobre 2026 par l’utilisateur Fantastic-Author2736, alias Sergious lorsqu’il enfile sa casquette de moddeur. La courte vidéo publiée permet de découvrir le jeu en vue à la première personne, avec un gameplay typique de Diablo, mais transposé en VR. « L’interface du jeu sort de l’écran pour s’afficher sur mon corps : l’inventaire à la ceinture, la carte dans la main, la barre d’outils sur le bras », précise le moddeur, qui incarne ici la Sorcière.
Diablo 2 en VR est un tout autre jeu
Fantastic-Author2736 explore ainsi les champs lugubres, armé de son bâton de sorcière et, on l’espère, d’un tube de médicaments contre la cinétose. Le voir lancer des boules de feu sur des ennemis qui rôdent à proximité est plutôt réjouissant avec ce point de vue inédit. Le système semble d’ailleurs plutôt bien fonctionner : la main gauche qui affiche la carte est une excellente idée, tandis que l’inventaire accessible à la ceinture est un ajout malin et logique.
Le mod propose en fait quatre vues : la caméra d’origine du jeu, affichée en vraie 3D ; une caméra libre derrière le héros ; le jeu posé sur le sol de votre pièce, en réalité mixte ; et la vue à la première personne montrée sur Reddit. Cette dernière reste un aperçu. D’après la page GitHub du projet, les armes ne sont pas encore calibrées, donc leur position dans les mains et leur visée peuvent être décalées.
Même sans être amateur de VR, on redécouvre l’univers de Diablo en le voyant à hauteur du personnage. Les décors prennent une toute autre dimension lorsque l’on peut réellement observer les alentours plutôt que de les surplomber. Les créatures semblent également plus imposantes lorsqu’elles apparaissent directement dans notre champ de vision.
Ce mod VR pour Diablo II: Resurrected est disponible gratuitement sur GitHub si vous souhaitez l’essayer. Pour jouer au casque, le mod passe par BodyWalk, un logiciel disponible sur Steam qui intègre FlatVR. Si vous ne l’avez pas, l’installateur ajoute une version gratuite, BodyWalk Lite. Il est aussi possible d’y jouer sans casque de réalité virtuelle, sur un écran classique, avec la souris et le clavier.
Il faut toutefois posséder Diablo II: Resurrected, le remaster développé par Vicarious Visions, et installer deux outils tiers : le lanceur D2RLoader et ReShade. Le mod est réservé au jeu solo hors ligne. Son auteur prévient qu’injecter du code dans le jeu en ligne peut faire bannir le compte. Il précise également que le projet n’a été ni conçu ni approuvé par Blizzard, qui devrait toutefois prendre quelques notes sur l’intérêt que la communauté porte déjà à une vue à la première personne.

articles.title: Qualcomm et ARM s'étrillent à nouveau devant la justice : le prix de votre prochain smartphone va-t-il augmenter ?
articles.text:
Qualcomm et Arm se retrouvent depuis lundi au tribunal fédéral de Wilmington, pour cinq jours d’audiences avec jury sous la présidence de la juge Maryellen Noreika. Cette fois, Qualcomm attaque : le concepteur des puces Snapdragon reproche à Arm des outils de test refusés malgré le contrat, et une fuite organisée autour de sa menace de résiliation de licence de 2024. En face, l’avocat d’Arm balaie d’une phrase : « ils n’ont pas subi le moindre préjudice ».
Cinq ans de redevances sur la table
La demande de Qualcomm donne l’échelle du dossier : suspendre jusqu’à cinq ans les redevances dues à Arm, soit plusieurs milliards de dollars. L’Américain pèse environ 9 % du chiffre d’affaires d’Arm sur son dernier exercice, et les deux maisons sont liées par contrat jusqu’en 2033. Qualcomm chiffre par ailleurs à 170 millions de dollars la valeur perdue sur un accord avec Meta à cause de la fuite de 2024, qu’il attribue à son adversaire. La juge n’a pas encore tranché la validité juridique de la clause de suspension invoquée.
Arm avait ouvert les hostilités en 2022, autour des licences héritées du rachat de Nuvia. Un jury a donné raison à Qualcomm en décembre 2024, un jugement final a confirmé cette victoire en septembre 2025, et Arm a fait appel dans la foulée. Un second procès se tient en parallèle, sans jury, pour examiner la bonne foi d’Arm dans la négociation des licences de prochaine génération. Qualcomm a aussi saisi les autorités de la concurrence en Europe, aux États-Unis et en Corée du Sud, où les bureaux d’Arm ont été inspectés fin 2025.
Des redevances enfouies dans chaque smartphone
Chaque puce Snapdragon embarque de la technologie Arm sous licence, et ces redevances entrent dans le coût des composants des téléphones Android, du milieu de gamme aux fleurons. Les cœurs maison issus du rachat de Nuvia, dont la licence a été validée par la justice fin 2024, irriguent les Snapdragon des prochaines générations, attendus dans les smartphones de 2027.
Aucun effet sur les prix ou la disponibilité n’est documenté à ce stade, et le verdict de 2024, sous réserve de l’appel en cours, a déjà sécurisé l’essentiel pour les puces actuelles. Le vrai enjeu pour l’acheteur se loge dans le procès parallèle : il porte précisément sur les conditions des licences de prochaine génération, celles qui fixeront le coût des puces de demain. Si les redevances bougent à l’issue du bras de fer, la facture des composants suivra, dans un sens ou dans l’autre.

articles.title: Ces lunettes affichent votre allure sans regarder votre montre
articles.text:
Engo Titanium : des lunettes de sport connectées de moins de 30 g
Les chiffres à l'oeil
Avec les Titanium, Engo affiche les données d'entraînement dans le champ de vision des coureurs et cyclistes. La marque grenobloise annonce un poids de 28,9 g et au moins 24 h d'autonomie, grâce notamment à des branches en titane.
Engo Eyewear engo Titanium
- 
                    
                        Xiaomi Smart Band 10 Meilleur prix : 46.99 €Voir le test
- 
                    
                        Google Fitbit Air Meilleur prix : 99.99 €Voir le test
- 
                    
                        Xiaomi Smart Band 9 Pro Meilleur prix : 49.99 €Voir le test
- 
                    
                        Garmin Vívosmart 5 Meilleur prix : 133.99 €Voir le test
Consulter son allure sans regarder sa montre est le principe des Engo Titanium. Ces lunettes connectées utilisent la technologie ActiveLook pour afficher la fréquence cardiaque, la cadence ou l'allure dans le champ de vision. Plus de 40 métriques sont proposées, avec une présentation personnalisable depuis l'application compagnon.
Des widgets permettent aussi de suivre des entraînements structurés, comme les séances de fractionné, et d'ajuster son rythme. De quoi garder ses données sous les yeux sans multiplier les coups d'oeil au poignet. La connexion passe par le Bluetooth, avec une compatibilité Garmin et d'autres appareils de l'écosystème ActiveLook, dont il faudra vérifier la liste avant l'achat.
Le titane fait le poids
Pour limiter la masse à 28,9 g, Engo utilise des branches en titane conçues et imprimées en 3D à Grenoble. Elles se règlent horizontalement et verticalement, tandis que le pont de nez est également ajustable.
L'équipement se concentre sur l'affichage : ni caméra, ni microphone, ni haut-parleurs. Le compteur reste donc dans les lunettes, la bande-son dans la tête. Engo annonce un écran OLED couleur lisible en plein soleil, une commande par double tap et au moins 24 h d'autonomie par charge.
Les Titanium sont proposées dès ce 6 octobre en édition limitée, exclusivement sur le site d'Engo. Comptez 599 € avec les verres standards et 649 € avec les verres photochromiques, qui adaptent leur teinte à la luminosité. Le poids s'allège donc, mais le portefeuille aussi.
